title: How Computer Networks & Routing Work Under the Hood ⚡
ig_caption:
How Computer Networks & Routing Work Under the Hood ⚡—what actually happens when you change your IP?
DNS lookup → sockets → AI vision of a cat (pixels → edges → verdict).

• Pixels in: the “cat” becomes numeric tensors (≈12M multiplications)
• Then: pixels → edges → parts (ears/eyes/whiskers) → verdict
• Under the hood: your network stack also does “layers”
• Routing: packets hop via next-hop decisions (not magic)
• DNS lookup: domain → IP so your app can connect
• TCP vs UDP: reliability vs low-latency delivery trade-off

Practical takeaway: When debugging, log the full path—DNS result, IP, socket type, and timing—before blaming the model.

Hot take: Is your AI “seeing” or just pattern-matching the same way routers “deliver” by rules—what breaks first when it fails?

fb_caption:
How Computer Networks & Routing Work Under the Hood ⚡ maps surprisingly well to how AI sees a cat.

When you watch the reel, the model’s pipeline is: pixels → edges → parts (ears/eyes/whiskers) → verdict. The networking pipeline has the same “layered” feel: name resolution → routing decisions → transport semantics → application processing.

Production trade-offs to notice:
• DNS lookup process: caching changes behavior dramatically (TTL, resolver choice, negative caching). Updating your IP doesn’t instantly change every client’s view.
• Routing: “it works” until path diversity, MTU, or next-hop selection fails; then packet loss looks like the system “can’t see.”
• TCP vs UDP: TCP’s handshake + retransmits add reliability; UDP favors low latency but pushes loss handling to the app.
• Layer boundaries: models fail when features don’t line up; systems fail when assumptions cross boundaries (e.g., wrong destination IP, wrong socket semantics).

Engineering patterns worth stealing:
• Instrument the chain end-to-end (DNS answer, resolved IP, connect/send timings, model confidence).
• Use explicit contracts at each layer: schema for inputs, clear retry/backoff policy for networking, deterministic logging for reproducibility.
• Build graceful fallbacks: circuit breakers for connectivity; confidence thresholds / fallback classifiers for vision.

If you’re interviewing: explain both pipelines using the same structure—“inputs, transformations, routing/aggregation, and final decision.” That’s a strong systems signal.

Curious question: when you change your IP or query DNS, what do you think breaks first—name resolution, routing, transport, or the app’s assumptions?
